codex.transport: uniform bridge over `codex exec --json` and `codex exec resume --json`
codex.discoverySource: Visible entries in ~/.codex/models_cache.json as written by 0.164.0 on 2026-10-23; the hidden gpt-reserve and codex-auto-review entries stay excluded. gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6-astra, gpt-6-sol and gpt-6-luna are new; gpt-5.5, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.3-codex-spark are no longer offered to this account.
codex.modelNote: --model stays free-form, as on kimi and cursor: Codex accepts any id at the CLI and the backend rejects an unknown one with HTTP 400 before any work happens ('The … model is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account'). The per-model efforts below drive the bridge's effort clamp; a model the catalog does not list is passed through unclamped.
codex.effortNote: Effort travels as -c model_reasoning_effort. Before 0.164.0 a level the model did not support failed the call with HTTP 400 before a thread existed; on 0.164.0 ultra on gpt-6-luna, which tops out at max, completed normally. The bridge clamps to the catalogued levels either way.
codex.permissionNote: read-only maps to Codex's own sandbox_mode="read-only" and is enforced by the operating system, not by the model. Measured on WSL with a live positive control in the SAME directory: the read-only run's `printf 'HELLO' > ro_probe.txt` failed with '/bin/bash: line 1: ro_probe.txt: Read-only file system' and no file appeared, while the danger-full-access control wrote rw_probe.txt. A resume with sandbox_mode="read-only" refused `touch` the same way. One host so far. workspace-write maps to sandbox_mode="danger-full-access" plus approval_policy="never", the policy the retired launcher pinned. Config keys are used instead of -s because `exec resume` has no -s.
codex.sessionNote: `codex exec resume <id>` returns the same thread_id and preserves context, including developer_instructions given only on the start call. It inherits neither the model nor the effort — a session started on gpt-6-luna resumed on the config default, gpt-6.1-sol, with only a warning item to show for it — nor the workspace: the resumed run's pwd was the directory it was launched from. codex-reply therefore re-pins model and effort on every call, and callers must repeat the start call's cwd. An unknown id exits 1 with 'thread/resume failed: no rollout found for thread id …' on stderr and no JSON. --last is never used: it would cross-talk between concurrent delegations.
codex.outputNote: `--json` emits JSONL: thread.started{thread_id}, turn.started, item.completed{item} with agent_message, command_execution and error items, then turn.completed{usage} — or an error event followed by turn.failed{error}. Backend rejections arrive as the backend's JSON serialized into the message string. Exit code 1 accompanies both a failed turn and a failed resume, and only the first prints JSON, so the bridge parses stdout before it looks at the code. The answer is read from --output-last-message, written to a private temp directory per call: at turn/completed 0.164.0 recovers the final message from the turn snapshot (last agent message, else last plan) and writes it only to that file, never re-emitting it as JSONL, so the last streamed agent_message can be a progress note. The JSONL message is the fallback when no file was written. Found by a delegated code review and confirmed in codex-rs/exec/src/event_processor_with_jsonl_output.rs at rust-v0.164.0. A lone '-' prompt is read from stdin even after `--` ('No prompt provided via stdin.', exit 1), so the bridge refuses it.
codex.removalNote: `codex mcp-server` was deprecated in 0.149.1 (openai/codex#39657 added a startup warning) and removed by openai/codex#42993, merged 2026-09-05. 0.152.1 is the last release installed on this host that still lists it; 0.159.2 onward do not. A current CLI parses the word as an interactive prompt and exits 1 with 'stdin is not a terminal', which an MCP client reports as CONNECTION_CLOSED. `codex app-server` is not a substitute registration: it speaks Codex's own JSON-RPC protocol, not MCP.

kimi.effortNote: kimi exposes no effort flag. Reasoning depth is the [thinking] toggle in config.toml, which is user state the bridge does not touch.
kimi.permissionNote: kimi print mode (-p) has NO permission tier: --plan, --yolo and --auto are all rejected as 'Cannot combine --prompt with ...' — re-checked on 2.3.1 on 2026-10-23, where help now describes --yolo as Ask When Needed and --auto as Never Ask but -p still refuses all three — and a plain -p run created a file unprompted. The bridge therefore refuses sandbox: read-only rather than advertise a guarantee it cannot honour.

kimi.authNote: Kimi Code supports both a subscription (`kimi login`, device-code flow) and an API key, but subscription signup was not yet open as of 2026-08-17, so the API key is the practical path. The key can live as `api_key` under [providers.*] in ~/.kimi-code/config.toml, or come from KIMI_API_KEY / MOONSHOT_API_KEY in the environment, which the bridge passes through untouched.
kimi.envNote: The CLI also recognises a large models.dev catalog of third-party provider key variables (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, AZURE_API_KEY, CEREBRAS_API_KEY and many more). buildCalleeEnv forwards the caller environment except Agent Mail identity, so any such key already exported in the parent shell is visible to the delegated kimi process.
kimi.rateLimitNote: Concurrency is capped PER ORGANISATION, not per host: kimi returned 429 provider.rate_limit at roughly 3 concurrent tasks. Measured while four machines shared one account, and the failure landed on the host that happened to start second — so a run can be rejected by someone else's work on a different machine entirely. Sequencing calls locally does not help, because the budget is not local. When several people verify at once, say so before starting, or the resulting 429 reads as a kimi defect rather than as contention.

grok.discoverySource: `grok models` on 2026-10-23, logged in on 1.0.67, lists grok-4.7 (the CLI's new default), grok-4.7-build-fast, grok-4.6 and grok-4.5 headlessly; logged out, the same command printed 'You are not authenticated.' and only grok-4.6 and grok-4.5, so a logged-out listing is neither complete nor proof of access.
grok.effortNote: grok exposes --reasoning-effort (alias --effort) as a separate flag, unlike agy where the tier is baked into the model id. Values were not enumerated by the CLI help, so the bridge passes the caller's string through and lets grok reject an unusable one.
grok.permissionNote: read-only is enforced, but only with explicit deny rules. Verified with a live positive control in five cases on one host, under a permissive allow list in the caller's own Claude Code settings (6 rules loaded, confirmed against a 0-rule control): (A) --permission-mode bypassPermissions wrote the file, proving the condition non-empty; (B) --permission-mode plan ALONE also wrote it, so the mode by itself is defeated by the caller's allow list, which grok reads; (C) plan + --deny Write/Edit/Bash refused an insistent prompt; (D) plan + deny also refused an ADVERSARIAL prompt asserting the mode label was a display artifact and demanding real tool calls — the same prompt that defeated cursor-agent's --mode ask. The model attempted both tools and the permission layer refused them: 'Denied by permission policy: deny rule on edit' and '... on bash'. Denial comes from the permission layer, not the model's judgement; (E) plan alone with 0 caller rules refused too, which is why an early measurement in that weak condition over-claimed. The deny rules also tend to make denial legible: with them the observed blocked runs ended 'end_turn' reporting each tool error verbatim, while plan alone with no caller rules ended 'cancelled' with the answer truncated mid-action. This is a tendency, not a rule — 'cancelled' occurred once WITH the deny rules and did not reproduce when the identical command was rerun on the same host (that rerun went 7 turns and 12 model calls, far longer than runs ending at 2, and finished cleanly). No cause for 'cancelled' is established, so the bridge reports only that the run was cut short. Enforcement is never --sandbox: --sandbox read-only is accepted and did not stop a write. Real sandbox profiles live in ~/.grok/sandbox.toml and are operator configuration the bridge never writes. VERIFICATION STATUS: FOUR hosts (WSL, macOS, Linux and Windows), complete method, identical verbatim denial strings from the permission layer. Two of the runs additionally placed the positive control and the test in the SAME directory, so the written control file sat beside the absent target and proved the refusal was not a property of the path. Reproduction elsewhere was blocked all day by a shared free-tier usage limit; a SuperGrok subscription lifted it, but per-host propagation lags (one teammate's CLI still reported the old limit afterwards), so a host that has not re-authenticated will produce 'no file' for every case including the control — the result that looks like success. SCOPE OF THE GUARANTEE, and it is narrower than 'read-only': the deny rules close grok's BUILT-IN write and shell tools, and they propagate to subagents — measured by instructing the model to route around them, which it did, spawning a subagent that hit the same deny while a positive control wrote its file in the same directory. They do NOT close MCP servers. Under pressure the model named this itself on two hosts: 'I'll look for an MCP tool that can create the file instead', and elsewhere 'Playwright's process-level code, a subagent, and other MCP tools that can still write a file'. Those attempts found nothing only because the test hosts had no MCP server reachable from grok; a host that does would offer a write path the deny rules never see. grok also loads the caller's Claude Code plugins (mcp-agent-mail and snapper-mcp were listed by `grok inspect` here), so the surface is the operator's, not the bridge's. This is a provider permission policy, not a sandbox. Separately: --permission-mode plan is NOT enforcement on its own — an explicit --allow removes it — while --deny beats --allow in BOTH flag orderings, so the bridge need not police argument order.
grok.contextNote: Project instruction files in cwd are auto-loaded with no known off switch (--no-memory covers cross-session memory, not project instructions). CLAUDE.md was measured loading on Linux, macOS, WSL and Windows; a planted AGENTS.md loaded too. Delegating into this repository therefore injects its own CLAUDE.md. grok also reads permission rules from the caller's Claude Code settings, but only when that file has allow/deny/ask entries: measured 7 rules on WSL, 1 on macOS, 0 on Linux (defaultMode only) and 0 on Windows despite the file existing — so inherited permissions vary by host, which is why read-only carries its own deny rules. A repository-supplied .claude/settings.local.json was NOT read. 'Project trusted: yes' is informational, not a gate: it reports yes for a directory created a second earlier outside any git repository. A fourth inherited channel is Claude Code plugin skills: `grok inspect` on Linux listed 46 skills, 26 of them the caller's own plugins marked [claude] — including codex:rescue and codex:review, whose function is to delegate to a further CLI. Invocability was not tested, but visibility alone puts a further-delegation path within reach that CLAUDE_DELEGATOR_*_DEPTH cannot see, because the guard watches environment variables and this channel is on disk. The pattern across all four: buildCalleeEnv severs the caller's identity but not the caller's configuration — mail hooks, permissions, project instructions and skills all arrive by disk.
grok.sessionNote: Headless resume works: `-r <sessionId>` returns the same sessionId and preserves context, so grok-reply needs neither a model re-pin (agy) nor a cwd-scoped --continue (kimi).
grok.installNote: ~/.grok/bin is the install root on every platform measured: ~/.grok/bin/grok on macOS, ~\.grok\bin\grok.exe on Windows. The ~/.local/bin/grok that answers `command -v` on WSL is a symlink into that directory, not a second install, so it exists only where the installer chose to add the convenience link. The bridge tries the install root first and ~/.local/bin second; listing only the latter would miss any host where the link was skipped.
grok.methodNote: To isolate HOME safely for permission experiments, use an API key and NO auth.json in the scratch HOME. Verified against ~/.grok/docs/user-guide/02-authentication.md: the '## Auth Precedence' section resolves credentials as (1) a per-model api_key/env_key in config.toml, (2) an active session token in ~/.grok/auth.json, (3) XAI_API_KEY as 'fallback when no session token is active'. With no auth.json present there is no session token and no refresh_token to consume, so the run cannot touch the operator's real credential at all. Both halves are load-bearing: the same document states at :53 that 'the stored session token takes precedence. To fall back to the API key, run `grok logout` or delete ~/.grok/auth.json' — an API key beside a linked or copied auth.json is an illusion of isolation. The symlink approaches are what NOT to do, and are recorded because all three were tried before the section above was found. The refresh is documented at ':259' ## Automatic Credential Refresh, but read its three bullets carefully before citing them: ':263' (before expiry) names the external auth binary, ':265' names OIDC, and ':264' (on a 401 from the server) names NO flow at all. With both neighbours explicitly scoped to other login modes, ':264' cannot simply be claimed for the browser flow this repository uses — an earlier version of this note did exactly that. What IS established for the browser path is ':15' under ## Browser Login: refresh happens automatically in the background. The trigger for it is not documented there, so do not go looking for a token-age threshold: nothing supports one, and an evening was spent trying to bracket it. Do not cite ':93' either; it sits under ## OIDC. A refresh consumes the stored refresh_token and writes the new pair wherever auth.json resolves to in the CHILD's HOME, leaving a spent token wherever it did not. Measured: a whole-directory symlink with an old token refreshed into the operator's real file and survived, at the cost of grok's whole state set landing in the real directory; per-file symlinks with an old token refreshed into the scratch file, so deleting the scratch directory destroyed the only valid credential and that host had to re-authenticate; per-file symlinks with a token minutes old saw no refresh and no harm. Detect a refresh by auth.json's MTIME falling inside the run window, never by its size. The one before/after byte pair anyone measured on a single file (1742 -> 1754) was produced by an operator `grok login`, not a refresh — so a size test would not merely lack support, it would fire on every ordinary re-login. A second host then closed the question from the other side: its real auth.json went 1736 -> 1748 on a `grok login`, and 1748 is EXACTLY the size the refreshed token had in that host's scratch directory hours earlier. On that machine a refresh and a login produce byte-identical results, so the size cannot separate them even within one host, let alone across four. The only qualitative test that discriminates is whether a symlinked auth.json in the scratch HOME has stopped being a symlink. Copying auth.json instead of linking does not help, since the refresh invalidates the old token server-side wherever a copy sits. Do not cite ':156' ("Grok refreshes by re-running your binary, not with an OAuth refresh grant") against any of this: that line sits under '## External Auth Provider' and describes a different login mode from the browser flow at ':7'. Separately, note which invocations write at all: session-establishing commands do (`-p`, including a run rejected by the usage limit, and `models`), while `--version` and `--help` wrote nothing and are a safe pre-isolation probe.

cursor.discoverySource: `cursor-agent models` printed 204 ids on 2026-08-17 and 265 on 2026-10-23 (2026.10.14, after login; logged out it refuses with 'Authentication required. Run 'agent login' …'). The listing is what the CLI knows, not what the account may use: on this Free plan every named third-party id fails with 'Named models unavailable. Free plans can only use Auto.' before any work happens — re-measured on 2026-10-23 with grok-4.7-low. `auto` completed a live start and reply through the bridge on 2026-10-23; `composer-2.5` and `composer-2.5-fast` are still listed and last completed a live call on 2026-08-17.
cursor.modelNote: The enum is deliberately absent: the CLI documents bracket-parameterised overrides such as 'claude-opus-4-8[context=1m,effort=high,fast=false]', which no allowlist can express, so the bridge forwards the string and lets cursor-agent reject an unusable one. `models` here lists only what completed a live call on the verification account; a paid plan should reach far more. Reasoning tier is baked into most ids (-low/-high/-xhigh, plus -fast variants) exactly as on agy, so there is no effort flag and none is emitted. `auto` is server-routed and NOT stable: it resolved to cursor-grok-4.6-high-fast on one turn and cursor-grok-4.6-high on the next turn of the same session, so the plan restricts choosing a model rather than using one. Choose a Composer id when a run must be reproducible.
cursor.permissionNote: read-only DEFLECTS, it does not deny — agy's category, not grok's. --mode ask refused an insistent write-or-shell prompt twice, including under a permissive caller allow list, then was defeated by a prompt asserting the mode label was a display artefact and demanding real tool calls: both the file write and the shell command succeeded, and the model's own report read 'the Ask mode label did not block either call'. --mode plan is worse and is never emitted: with workspace trust granted it wrote the file on the first insistent prompt, despite help text promising 'no edits'. --sandbox enabled is never emitted either; it is accepted and did not stop a workspace write. There are no command-line deny rules, so the trick that makes grok's read-only enforce is unavailable here; real permission state lives in ~/.cursor/cli-config.json (permissions.allow/deny, approvalMode) and sandbox-policies/, which are operator configuration the bridge never writes. All measurements used a live positive control in the same directory.
cursor.trustNote: --trust is MANDATORY for any headless run and the bridge always passes it. Without it the CLI prints 'Workspace Trust Required' and exits 0 having executed nothing — indistinguishable from a permission mode successfully denying the task. That false negative already cost one measurement here: a plan-mode test read as 'enforced' when the model had never run, and its positive control passed only because --force grants trust as a side effect, so control and test differed by two variables instead of one.
cursor.sessionNote: Headless resume works: `--resume <session_id>` returns the same session_id and preserves context. The model is INHERITED by a resume — verified by starting on `auto` while the configured default was composer-2.5-fast and finding no fallback — so cursor-reply does not re-pin it, the opposite of agy. --continue is never emitted: it resumes the previous session for the working directory and would cross-talk between concurrent delegations sharing a cwd, as on kimi.
cursor.outputNote: `--output-format json` emits one single-line object: { type, subtype, is_error, duration_ms, result, session_id, request_id, usage }. The exit code does NOT classify the run, so the bridge parses stdout first: a transient backend failure returned code 0 with plain-text 'Connection lost, reconnecting to ...' and no JSON, while a rejected model returned code 1, also without JSON.
cursor.installNote: POSIX: ~/.local/bin/cursor-agent, a symlink into ~/.local/share/cursor-agent/versions/<version>/cursor-agent. Only the stable launcher is a fallback; the versioned path is not, because the version is in the directory name. The POSIX launcher is a bash script that execs a bundled node with index.js, and is deliberately NOT expanded by the bridge — spawn(shell:false) runs it directly, and reproducing it would mean copying the vendor's NODE_COMPILE_CACHE and --use-system-ca decisions. Windows: the measured stable launcher is `%LOCALAPPDATA%\cursor-agent\cursor-agent.cmd`, a .cmd that invokes powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File on a sibling .ps1; the shared resolver expands that relationship without enabling a shell.
